The GRAVITY instrument at the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) stands as a four-telemeter beam combiner utilizing four Merlier-Len (MELI) cameras. Each camera features two HgR-5833 photomultiplier tubes positioned behind Brewster-angle glass plates, which are optimized for detecting the interferometric signature by recording only the carrier-suppressed fringe pattern. This analysis details the performance evaluation of the GRAVITY gathering system, noting that while three fully equipped modules met specifications, the fourth required minor upgrades. Consequently, GRAVITY now gathers light from three beam-position monitors and four beam-loss monitors, ensuring precise alignment and monitoring of incoming beams throughout all interferometric observations.

This paper investigates the distinction between "freeway dimension" and "Euclidean doubling dimension" within the context of metric spaces, analyzing how these properties influence the complexity of algorithms for generalized $k$-center and related problems. We establish that the freightway dimension can exceed the Euclidean doubling dimension by as much as a square root of two, and establish that the freightway dimension may be unbounded even when Euclidean doubling remains finite. In instances where Euclidean doubling is finite but freeway highway is infinite, the graph of $\epsilon$-freeway is shown to be tree-like for sufficiently small $\epsilon$, thereby supporting a constant-factor approximation of the optimal objective. Conversely, when Euclidean routes are finite but freeway highways are infinite, the graph of $\epsilon$-freeway may possess an unbounded path length for any fixed $\epsilon$, resulting in the impossibility of achieving an approximation with a constant factor. These results are substantiated by novel counterexamples.

In 2000, S. Bhoje and G. G. Stenger established that if a linear difference quotient of an entire function shares a TIBL (Totally Bounded by Logarithm) small function with its original function, then that entire function is a polynomial. Expanding on this work, our paper presents several new findings regarding polynomial characterizations of entire functions defined by the relation between an function and its two-point shift. We also provide specific examples and present several counter-examples to explore the boundary conditions of our theorems. Furthermore, we prove several theorems concerning the uniqueness of entire functions determined by their linear difference equations with distinct polynomial coefficients.

A critical challenge in solving multivariate polynomial systems is the prevalence of erroneous data, which renders traditional elimination and Gröbner basis methods often impractical. This study offers a novel approach specifically designed to handle systems containing inaccuries, with a primary focus on the pivotal intermediate step known as polynomial degree reduction (PDR). The new method employs an over-determined linear system to minimize deviation caused by mistakes; however, this system often exhibits full density and lacks sparsity. Consequently, we introduced a novel algorithm with essentially linear complexity for resolving PDR within such non-sparsely structured environments and proved its correctness by providing a uniqueness upper bound. This limit, derived using the Schwartz-Zippel lemma, demonstrates that for a sufficient number of sample points, the underlying exact linear system can be accurately recovered even when noisy observations prevent direct solution. Since this bound also dictates when the augmented system effectively mirrors the original system with only minimal noise interference, it enables an early termination strategy: computation can cease as soon as the bound is reached, thereby substantially boosting performance on instances with redundant but imperfect data.

A particle package is defined as a collection of particles that share specific kinematic traits, such as moving together as a coherent group. Recently, researchers have proposed a method to classify packages based on their momentum configurations, utilizing both Momentarily Collinear configurations (MTCs) and Momentarily Uniform configurations (MUCs). While this approach effectively captures many observed packages, numerous others—particularly jets exhibiting axial symmetry—were not explained. This study introduces a new criterion for identifying Axially Symmetric configurations (ASCs). Notably, particle systems within these jets often maintain the simultaneous validity of both parity symmetry and ASCs, creating a unique paritality-conserving subset. We have developed an efficient algorithm to compute a Parity-Symmetry-Preserved Package Emission function (Parity-Sym-Pers-Pak-PE), denoted as $\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{psp}(\theta,\phi)$. This function quantifies how closely particle arrangements within a given jet approximate a parity-conserving package emission model. These metrics are now available in the modernizing HEPS (Modern Particle Physics) Software Library.

We introduce a simplified yet precise analytical model describing how matter behaves at extreme compression and high temperatures found in the interiors of giant gas planets and large moons like Io. Based on first principles and within the framework of statistical mechanics for charged matter, we find that even in the highest thermal states, Coulomb interactions remain critical for determining the state equation and core properties of these bodies. Using this new formalism, we derive clear expressions for the equation of state and related thermodynamic potentials of an ideal-free electron-protone plasma augmented by heavier alkali elements (specifically those with a single valence electron). Our derived model for an equation of state effectively captures the intricate interplay between the Coulomb forces characteristic of highly compressed alkali metals and the Pauli exclusion principles governing neutral atoms. We evaluate the validity ranges of this approach by comparing it to established equations of state in the non-ideal regime and by referencing recent **ab initio** simulations performed on potassium plasma.

This study investigates the spectral properties of light vector mesons within a background exhibiting chiral asymmetry, referring to an environment where left- and right-handed fermions exhibit unequal densities. Utilizing a 2+1 dimensional quantum electrodynamics (QED-2+1) model, we explore how this imbalance influences both finite temperature and pressure conditions, as well as various media flows, using a Higgs mechanism that generates vector meson mass. We compute the spectral function by analyzing the polarization tensor at one-loop order, incorporating Landau damping effects via the Pauli matrix. Furthermore, we construct the constituent quark mass profile by solving the gap equation within this medium. Finally, we examine how the resulting medium properties affect the mass shifts and widths of light vector mesons in their constitutive spectrum.

This study addresses a fundamental task in network computation—estimating network size ($n$)—within a model where some nodes are Byzantine (arbitrarily faulty). We operate under the premise of small-world networks characterized by high sparsity and low-degree high-girth expander backbones, which facilitate rapid message mixing. In this environment, a subset of nodes attempts to deceive others, while honest nodes aim to accurately estimate $n$. Building on prior research, which achieved an $\tilde{O}(n)$ sample scale estimation for fault-free small-world networks, our approach quantifies the impact of adversarial nodes. Specifically, we demonstrate that with a fraction $\epsilon$ of faults present:
1. If $\epsilon < 0.25$, there exists a protocol allowing honest nodes to estimate $n$ within a multiplicative factor of $\epsilon/1$ using $\tilde{O}(n/\epsilon^2)$ samples.
2. If $\epsilon \le 0.25$, honest nodes can achieve an $\tilde{O}(1)$ scale estimate (essentially constant scale accuracy) with only $\tilde{O}(\epsilon n)$ samples.
These findings establish a critical tradeoff between sample efficiency and the precision of the scale estimate. We prove this relationship is optimal up to logarithmic terms, thereby defining the performance boundaries of estimating the size of large-scale networks in the presence of Byzantine failures.

We introduce an innovative method for solving the constraint equations of numerical relativity on unstructured grids. The proofreading process begins with the spatial slicing defined by the shift and lapse, followed by fixing the trace of the extrinsic stress, followed by solving the traceless Weyl equation. A key advantage of the technique is its ability to handle equations with complicated coefficients and boundaries on any arbitrary mesh. Additionally, it employs an adaptive strategy for selecting numerical approaches to the problem at hand. We validate our approach by comparing numerical results to known analytical solutions. Finally, we illustrate how this framework can help resolve open questions regarding the existence of solutions to constraint equations.

Predicting multivariate time series is a critical challenge across numerous fields, yet existing methods often fail to consider the distinct, high-dimensional characteristics of the data. To overcome this, we introduce a novel Adaptive graph convolutional network (AGCN) designed specifically for time series forecasting. The method innovates by constructing an adaptive, hierarchical network architecture that mirrors the data's higher dimensions: the first layer identifies local long-term temporal dependencies, the intermediate layers detect further hierarchical time series patterns, and the final layer extracts global time series features. Additionally, we define a "Gated Graph Linear Unit" in each layer, which regulates node and edge weights through a gating mechanism to mitigate over-smoothing issues prevalent in convolutional methods. This unit also enhances model expressivity by independently and sparsely activating specific layers and connections based on task requirements. Extensive validation on three datasets containing eight multidimensional time series tasks demonstrates that AGCN significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines.

A comprehensive suite of models has been developed to simulate light propagation through the lower atmospheric layers, specifically the troposphere and stratosphere. The model incorporates ray tracing calculations and computes attenuation via absorption and scattering mechanisms. It further evaluates radiative effects, including atmospheric polarization and atmospheric polarization anisotropy. This suite has been integrated into the measurement tools and data analysis software, forming a critical component of new technologies designed for atmospheric correction. These tools enable precise characterization of the atmosphere, which is increasingly essential for observational strategies targeting the Sun, the Moon, stars, the Milky Way, quasars, and galactic nuclei, as well as for future missions like the Euclid project. Consequently, these tools will be increasingly valuable for techniques relying on spatial and spectral image deconvolution, and especially for high-contrast imaging techniques such as direct exoplanet detection.

Recently, pre-training has enabled large-scale models to reach human-level performance, resulting in an expansive ecosystem of specialized fine-tuned variants for tasks like object detection. This diversity often complicates the selection of optimal models for specific applications. Knowledge Distillation offers a solution by ensemble-ing multiple models into an integrated system, though this approach is frequently hindered by the high computational cost of ensemble training. This paper presents Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), a novel knowledge distillation framework based on pairwise comparison iterations that avoids the need for an explicit teacher network. Instead, it iteratively refines a set of student networks by using the composite loss function, where loss is dynamically re-calculated based on the evolving performance of the student ensemble itself. This iterative refinement continues until convergence, effectively distilling inter-student knowledge into the final students. Notably, this method minimizes computational overhead since the ensemble is trained once on student networks, rather than incurring repeated retraining costs associated with teacher ensembles. Experiments utilizing state-of-the-art detectors—ResNet-FPN and RetroDet—across COCO and Visual Decog tests demonstrate that PILE significantly outperforms standard non-iterative ensemble training while requiring far fewer resources.

Current theories posit that a significant portion of dark matter may be bosonic rather than purely fermionic, a possibility attributable to an as-yet-undetected component known as "shadow matter." This specific fraction could exist as ultralight bosons interacting via weak intensities through interferometric signatures. This study investigates such particles using intensity interferometry, a technique capable of probing frequencies in the petahertz range by analyzing the fluctuating intensities of sunlight. Based on contemporary observations, our results establish exclusion limits for ultralight bosons with masses below $10^{-14}$ eV, specifically within the $\phi-SS$ (where S represents spin-0 or spin-1) coupling context.

This paper investigates a Basis Pursuit formulation within a continuum setting, applied to determine material properties like density and expansion coefficients. We analyze a convex optimization problem involving control variable densities and these coefficients, constrained by a data fidelity term based on an integral operator and a total variation regularizer. By examining the associated KKT conditions, we establish sufficient criteria to prove uniqueness. Specifically, in the lossless case where measurements are perfectly consistent with a material property model, unique recovery is guaranteed when material densities are strictly positive and uniquely determined if the support of the unknown functions is a a.a.t. We further demonstrate that, under lossy conditions, unique reconstruction is possible provided there are no resonances among the basis functions. Finally, reconstruction errors are bounded in terms of the input data.

The P4 language, a widely adopted solution for writing programmable switches, primarily functions as an independent, language-agnostic specification where specific compilation toolchains for various hardware platforms remain a limiting factor. This study introduces an open-source P4 compiler backend dedicated to reconfigurable match-per-group (MPG) table switches, which utilize a separate MPG stage to manage group actions within standard P4 match-based tables. This architectural approach streamlines the logic complexity often found in modern, high-performance switch specifications, which can otherwise become unwieldy. By leveraging the internal switch logic, a simple configuration process applies grouped execution policies, significantly reducing the programming overhead compared to manually mapping individual actions to multiple tables. To validate the feasibility of P4 specifications on MPG architectures, we developed a comprehensive toolchain compatible with V1-Main, 1.4, and 1.5 (of the V1 model), allowing the simulation of these designs on the industry-leading Broadcom TomoX2 platform. This research provides a robust foundation for both the evolution of the P4 language and the expansion of its supporting ecosystem.

A common approach for modeling surface transport phenomena involves discretizing the divergence-free transport equation using the Raviart-ARTIartian element with minimal polynomial degree on quadrilateral meshes. To address potential accuracy issues that may arise specifically for the transport component of such discretizations, we introduce a correction method. This technique involves solving an auxiliary equation on the same element type to yield an adjusted solution with marked improvements. We demonstrate the optimality of this strategy through applications involving surface transport and surface-wind-driven transport. These latter simulations are implemented via direct Python integrations of the stream function on the solution vectors, thereby validating the method's efficacy by confirming the divergence-free nature of the results.

The established body of research confirms that deep neural networks can exhibit significant biases, causing issues with health care, criminal justice, and hiring practices. While differential privacy (DP) limits the inference of individual training data, the extent to which this privacy guarantee also ensures fairness has not been adequately studied. This work establishes a theoretical link between DP and fairness, providing the first such relationship while also accounting the specific constraints imposed by federated learning. We demonstrate that, under the assumption of a Gaussian shift distribution among clients, the number of participating parties directly influences both the achieved fairness level and the achievable privacy bounds. Additionally, we designed the first practical mechanism to identify and mitigate biases within this federated setting, theoretically proving its ability to remove biases without compromising established privacy guarantees. The presented theory offers the following contributions: it demonstrates that, given a specific information budget, the presence of bias indicates a failure to fully achieve fairness; consequently, enhancing the inference capabilities of a model directly threatens the privacy of individual contributors. We further show that both fair treatment and robust privacy are only theoretically guaranteed when contributions from a consistent number of parties are aggregated. This leads to the surprising result that federated learning cannot ensure the simultaneous protection of individual user data and equitable treatment unless it involves pooling data from a minimum threshold of participants, beyond which these concerns can be satisfied. We report the observation of excited $B_c^+$ states within the $K^+\pi^+\pi^-$ and $K^+\pi^+K^-$ final states, utilizing proton-proton collision datasets collected by the LHCb detector at center-of-mass energies of 7, 8, and 13 TeV, as identified via tracks with pseudorapidity $2 < \theta^* < 5$. The recorded integrated luminosities were 1.0 fb$^{-1}$, 1.36 pb$^{-1}$, and 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ respectively, yielding an observed signal significance of 9.2σ. The measured masses for the $K^+\pi^+ \pi^0$ system in the $K^+\pi^+ \pi^0$ channel are 3.621±0.003±0.002 GeV/$c^2$ and 3.621±0.003±0.002 GeV/$c^2$, respectively, with corresponding significances of 9.2σ and 9.1σ. The first value corresponds to a state with a width of 0.012±0.001±0.001 GeV, while the second to one with a width of 0.012±0.001±

This study introduces continuous-runge-Kutta schemes for approximating nonlinear and linear differential equations for $y'=f(y)$, where $f$ is either nonlinear, linear, or a combination. These methods utilize a Runge-Kutta scheme as the integrator along the $s$ abscissa quadrature rules, where the number of stages matches the number of quadrature stages. Schemes for these continuous-runge-Kutta methods, including the Runge-Kutta schemes, are discussed, along with their stability and convergence. For stable schemes, the continuous-runge-Kutta methods converge to order $s$ for $s \ge 1$. As a special case, the continuous-runge-Kutta methods based on the Runge-Kutta schemes are shown to have the same order of stability as the Runge-Kutta schemes used to solve the problems for $s \ge 1$.

Achieving breakthroughs in computer vision and image recognition often depends on massive neural networks coupled with enormous datasets; however, these scales create significant challenges regarding training time and inference latency. As hardware continues to scale up regionally with interconnects that increasingly outnumber intra-processor communication channels, optimizing training efficiency becomes even more critical. Although methods like adversarial training have enhanced neural networks for tasks such as image generation and recognition, they frequently suffer from unstable training dynamics and diminished performance in large network scenarios. To address this, we introduce a new approach that enhances adversarial training specifically for large networks by leveraging regional critical mass and regional gradient techniques. RegLoss is simpler to implement than standard VAE training and outperforms multiple baseline techniques on sample quality and stability. Furthermore, our experiments indicate a significant stability improvement, allowing large network training to complete in roughly half the time under the same conditions.

Recent investigations into the chaotic scattering of ellipsoidal billiard systems in 2D and co-orbital dynamics of charged particles around two stars in 3D have revealed that dissipative forces can significantly alter or even invert scattering outcomes. This study demonstrates similar sensitivity to dissipation in the context of the double-pulse potential (DPP), a simplified model of a complex, naturally occurring environment. We investigate how non-conservative forces within the chaotic scattering of the DPP lead to the emergence of novel dynamical phenomena, notably an increase in the fractal dimension of Wada boundaries—a specific configuration where attractors share common, continuous phase-space separators. While conserved-energy trajectories in the DPP display 3-percolating Wada basins involving just two attractors, imposing weak dissipation on this system not only stabilizes these Wada regions but also triggers a sudden drop in Lyapunov exponents, thereby extending a newly formed, third fractal basin into existence. These observations offer fresh perspectives on dynamical structures arising in astrophysical contexts.

We examine a model featuring three right-handed neutrinos, which generate both right-handed isospin symmetry and light, flavor-changing bosons. Although these bosons mediate low-energy contact interactions modifying processes such as $\mu \to e\gamma$, their gauge non-copiecality endows them with extended lifetimes, enabling the observation of decays like $B^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ (or $B^0_s \to \mu^+ \mu^$). We demonstrate that, following the measurement of the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron ($g-2$), one can establish the parameter-space constraints. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of various decay channels, specifically noting sensitivity from recent searches at LHCb and proposing dedicated searches at a future factory.

Accumulating interest in activity recognition in videos stems from its vital role in monitoring human behavior, an application crucial for medical, military, and security purposes however. Although many current methods depend heavily on annotated instance trajectories or extensive annotated training datasets which are difficult to obtain for real-world video surveillance data. To address this limitation, an new hierarchical attention network that requires no trajectory annotations has been introduced in our work while effectively integrating spatial and temporal attention mechanisms which improve the model's ability to capture important regions within video frames and distinguish key temporal segments. Extensive evaluations across three public video datasets demonstrate that this proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art trajectory-based activity recognition systems.

This work explores the dynamics of scalar fields near the horizon of Reissner-Nordstr$\ddot{o}$m anti-de Sitter black holes within the framework of scalar-tensor-vector-supergravity. First, we determine the specific charge-to-height ratio required for a test particle to come to a rest exactly at the horizon. Subsequently, we investigate the thermodynamic characteristics of the resulting daughter black hole. Finally, by testing particle trajectories with varying velocities before falling into the black hole, we examine whether the feeble conspiracy censorship conjecture holds in this context.

This work examines the physical mechanisms behind how stars form. It examines a star's life cycle from its initial gravitational collapse through to supernova explosions, offering a fundamental physics-based understanding of these phenomena via theoretical models complemented by observational data and numerical simulations.

The nested sampling algorithm originally designed to solve or estimate the partition function, can also determine the Gibbs-Shannon (GS) entropy directly from the algorithm's trajectory. This method proves more efficient than post-algorithm calculations that rely on the 'quenched' and 'annealed' approximations, particularly when these limitations stem from the heavy computational cost associated with sampling from high-dimensional integrals, such as those found in models like the Potts system. By utilizing a computational pathway based on a pseudo-Taylor series expansion of the cumulative free energy, we find that the GS entropy derived via nested sampling aligns very closely with entropy estimates obtained using Nudged Elastic Chain Molecular Dynamics (NEC-MD). However, it is important to note that while the nested sampling technique calculates both GS entropy and the corresponding thermodynamic heat capacity, these outputs may suffer from large statistical uncertainties near phase transitions due to sampling variance.

We analyze the validity of certain weak solutions for a specific hyperbolic conservation law featuring discontinuous, bounded coefficients. By relying on a novel class of solutions known as "feeble measures," we broaden the criteria, demonstrating that measure-valued solutions meet the requirements. This finding extends beyond earlier constraints regarding coefficient regularity. Furthermore, our results establish that for a given set of inputs, essentially only one solution exists in both $L^{1}$ and $\mathcal{M}$-- this uniqueness holds true except under the measure $\nu$ where it is null.

Detecting intrusions in network security is a critical area of study. While previous research has primarily focused on intrusion systems for high-end hardware, there is a growing need for solutions tailored to resource-constrained IoT devices. These systems often suffer from limited RAM and processing power, making the execution of complex machine learning models impractical. To address this, we introduce NB coded, a specialized detection architecture designed to operate efficiently within the strict resource constraints of IoT environments. We evaluated the system using the Linux-based BEETLE IoT device, which features only 512 KB of RAM and 250 MHz CPU speed, analyzing its performance across various network assault scenarios. Results demonstrate that with a dataset of 10,000 samples, the system achieves 99.99% accuracy. Furthermore, the model's memory consumption remains stable at approximately 280 MB regardless of the dataset's size.

We provide nearly tight upper limits on the expansion rates of activities within a finite solvable group $G$. Specifically, we define the activity $act_G(G/H)$ arising from a subgroup index $[G:H]$, and our main finding shows that for the largest possible subgroup of $G$, this expansion occurs at a rate bounded above by $O(\log^2 |G|)$. Furthermore, we identify scenarios where the growth achieves the lowest complexity possible, scaling instead at $O(\log^3 |G|)$; indeed, such scenarios hold true for the group of upper triangular matrices with entries in $\mathbb{Z}_p$ (where $p$ is a prime). The final section examines specific $p$ groups, determining the expansion laws that follow from taking normal subgroups indexed by $p$.

Tracking dynamic processes within microscopic cellular environments is vital for understanding fundamental biological mechanisms like growth and metabolism, yet this remains difficult due to the chaotic thermal motion (Brownian noise) that obscures the paths of microscale particles. This study introduces a computational strategy designed to distinguish and follow the trajectories of particles undergoing active transport, regardless of their scale. The method operates by first extracting particle positions from digital videos, then utilizing statistical properties of velocity autocorrelation functions to detect continuous movements belonging to the same entity. Furthermore, these tracked paths are agglomerated into broader collections, enabling the visualization of probability density maps that reveal the specific dynamics under investigation. Validation experiments utilized simulated data based on real experimental footage of fluorescent-labeled bacteria moving within a mucociliary system; results confirmed the method's robust performance in accurately recovering true trajectories and generating reliable density maps. Additionally, a dedicated open-source tool implementing this technique has been created and made publicly available.

Optimizing stateless vector quantum computers holds promise for advancing various fields, including financial planning, drug discovery, and machine learning. Beyond these areas, the potential of quantum computing for optimizing energy grids remains largely unexplored. This paper examines the most critical and pressing need in the smart grid network: the optimization of transmission lines to minimize the cost of delivering electricity from generation sources to consumers. Consequently, this work outlines and implements a solution leveraging the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) algorithm, incorporating recently developed cost function variations within the VQE framework. These new formulations address the inherent difficulties of minimizing energy delivery costs. The study concludes by reporting quantum circuit implementations, simulated through both IBMQ and Rigorous quantum devices, and analyzes their performance.

Machine learning offers powerful tools for extracting physical insights from vast datasets, a capability shared across theoretical and experimental physics. A key advantage of these approaches is their ability to uncover fundamental principles of nature; yet, existing literature often fails to explain the underlying mechanisms of such discoveries. This review presents a unifying framework for understanding the nature of these intellectual breakthroughs by formalizing them as finding low-dimensional structures within high-dimensional data spaces. We illustrate this concept through concrete cases across physical domains, including the identification of hadron resonances from scattering phase shifts, the U(1)D symmetry emerging from the fractional quantum Hall effect data, the deconfined gauge symmetry proposed in numerics for the Hubbard model, and the universal laws connecting black hole geometry to their electromagnetic fields. Finally, we address common challenges including the stochastic variability of selected structures, difficulties in model interpretability, and the risk of hallucinations.

This analysis details a search conducted by the ATLAS detector at the LHC for potential heavy, electrically charged particles with lifetimes exceeding the picosecond scale ($\tau > 10$ ps) produced in $pp$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. The study utilizes a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 36.0 fb$^{-1}$ collected by ATLAS at a proton-proton collision energy of 13 TeV. The search targets particles with electric charges significantly different from the unit charge ($|Q| \gg 1$), which exhibit a marked deviation in how their specific ionization energy decreases as they traverse detector material compared to minimum ionizing particles. This investigation covers the mass spectrum from 1 to 2 TeV and proper lifetimes ranging from $1$ cm to $10^6$ cm. The findings are consistent with the Standard Model background expectations, and the results are expressed as 95% confidence level exclusion limits covering a wide mass-lifetime parameter space.

This paper reports on ridge-waveguide-based quantum dot cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED) in integrated devices, achieving high performance through the strong light-matter interaction inherent to the system. We demonstrate that our source emits narrow linewidth single photons with a coherence time extending beyond 3 microseconds. Characterization via the second-order correlation function reveals near-efficacious performance, with $g^{(2)}(0)$ below 1% at an extracted efficiency of approximately 75%. These results represent the most favorable properties to date for an on-chip single-photon source.

Inelastic neutron scattering studies offer a comprehensive view of both long- and short-range structural dynamics through the measurement of the dynamical structure factor, $S(Q, \omega)$. This work examines the time domain counterpart, the partial Van Hove function, $G_s(\alpha R, t)$. While the authors utilize the invariant spectral density, $I(\alpha R, t) = \alpha t G_s(\alpha R, t) / \pi$, to reveal atom-specific short-range temporal - long-range spatial correlations known as the boson peak, they demonstrate how to extract such long-lived anomalies lasting hundreds of picoseconds from systems exhibiting glassy behavior. These findings stem from time-domain simulations of neutron scattering off model liquids composed of hard spheres alongside molecular dynamics simulations targeting amorphous silica.

The paper examines the multi-loop, multi-scale Feynman diagrams essential for achieving high-precision physics. We aim to calculate these complex configurations for Higgs boson production via the process $\pp \to hh$. This analysis covers relevant topologies ranging from two-loop to five-loop diagrams containing three to five scales. The investigation encompasses both Abelian and non-Abelian gauge theories within the Standard Model, as well as Qudos box and graph configurations involving light fermions. Hints for potential computational strategies to master these intricate graph topologies are also identified.

Supplementing our recent work on \arxiv{10.1103/PhysRevLett.131.201101,10.1103/PhysRevLett.131.201101}, this study examines the energy deposition formed by summation of eigenchannels within scattering systems. While these concepts have previously been explored mainly within nuclear physics, this article investigates the inherent relations governing the matrix elements connecting the kinetic and energy deposition versions of eigenchannels, thereby establishing connections between various observables derived from the elemental scattering process.

We identified a previously unknown spiral arm located in the galaxy's outer regions, utilizing data from the HI Line Survey of the Netherlands (VLA). This newly discovered arm, designated the Far 3-Kpc Arm, was found by examining a continuous HI emission feature in the outer Galaxy that connects the Norma and Perseus arms. Although the Perseus arm is known to extend across the galactic disk, the Far 3-Kpc Arm is a distinct formation situated in the outer 3 kpc. The arm lies between right ascension (RA) coordinates of 1$^h$ and 2$h$. Data from the VLA reveal that the arm is roughly 2 kpc long, spans a width of roughly half that length, and extends about 3 degrees in height. The increasing adoption of high-throughput experimental techniques in biological research has driven a critical demand for optimization strategies capable of preserving biodiversity within ecosystems. Similarly, agricultural practices necessitate methods that maintain genetic heterogeneity to foster resilience against diseases and pathogens, thereby securing food security. While these biological objectives have spurred growing interest in Multi-Objective Optimization, there is currently limited understanding of how to implement Multi-Objective Optimization across the fields of biology and agriculture. This paper introduces a methodology to quantify phenotypic diversity—optimizing for both fitness and diversity simultaneously. We demonstrate the validity of this approach using a model system based on a host-parasite interaction.

The concept of the Stable Roommates Problem involves assigning unpaired participants within a single group so that no two individuals believe they would be better matched with each other than their current assignment. In its standard formulation, these individuals express strict rankings of all other group members regarding whom they would most prefer to pair with. However, many real-world pairing scenarios allow for more flexibility; for instance, in challenge contexts, some participants may prefer remaining unpaired over a specific pairing options. Consequently, these individuals possess detailed, though not necessarily strict, preferences regarding every available option either to pair up or stay solo. This variability complicates stability assessments, as multiple types of stable outcomes can emerge. This variability makes certain output solutions more resistant to manipulation than others. We introduce a comprehensive theoretical framework to investigate how sound waves interact with valley electrons in two-dimensional systems. Finally, these theoretical predictions are compared against experimental data from graphene to evaluate their relevance.

Stable quantum computation demands fault tolerance because individual components face high error rates and are unreliable. We introduce two reinforcement learning (Rl) generated algorithms designed to build fault-tolerant quantum computers by assembling specialized super circuits from basic hardware blocks. The first approach optimizes an optimization-based score, aiming to shorten gate sequences while minimizing both circuit depth and connectivity constraints. The second employs a neural network to classify circuits as viable or not, leveraging data derived from noisy computation outcomes. We demonstrate, through experiments on both simulated and real quantum hardware using qubit counts ranging from 5 to 11, that this RL framework successfully generates viable fault-tolerant solutions that outperform current state-of-the-art methodologies in specific scenarios.

We introduce an interferometric scheme centered on connected cavities that enables precision measurements reaching Heisenberg scaling, where measurement accuracy improves inversely with the total number of involved particles. This protocol utilizes shared entangled states within the cavities to create a two-partition quantum metrology approach. Initially, increasing precision is achieved by entangling more than two particles at the first measurement stage. Subsequently, precision enhances through linking cavities via the second stage: performing individual measurements within each cavity after performing a beam splitter operation between them. We demonstrate the validity and efficacy of this two-partition technique through various numerical models. These results include applications of quantum metrology principles to analyze a two-cavity system operating with both coherent Squeezed Schemes and Fock states as input.

The STAR collaboration reports findings from direct photon-hadron association measurements within $d$$+$Au and Au$+$Au collision events at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV, alongside comparable results from $p$$+$Au collisions. The experiments utilized $1$-jet and $2$-jet and photon-hadron correlation techniques to probe both high-$p$$+{}$T, hard-scattering-driven photon-hadron associations and the medium's response to high-$p$$+{}$T fragments. In the $d$$+$Au configuration, no significant evidence for enhanced photon-hadron correlations indicative of nuclear modifications has been found. Conversely, in Au$+$Au collisions, the correlation functions display a suppression at higher transverse photon energies that converges with predictions from hydrodynamic models at lower photon energies.

To advance the development of quantum algorithms addressing many-body physics phenomena, we introduce a systematic framework rooted in the symmetries of target Hamiltonians. This approach integrates an analog evolution step, driven by Hermitian operators—specifically those Hermitian and anti-Hermitian—which preserve the target Hamiltonian’s symmetries, with discrete digital quantum control encoded via a minimal set of logical qubits. We demonstrate that this scheme applies to fermionic systems, allowing the Hamiltonians to be Hermitian or anti-Hermitian transformed into forms suitable for simulation using hybrid digital–analog techniques. Furthermore, using a digital quantum approach, we investigate the dynamics of spin orbit coupling within an artificial quantum dot, transforming these into Hermitian or anti-Hermitian forms as needed for simulation. Transverse-field Ising models with various interactions are similarly transformed for efficient quantum emulation. Finally, we show that this flexible, robust framework supports diverse physical models, making them accessible even to quantum processors with limited but improving qubit counts.

This study introduces a construction method for pseudo-features aimed at enhancing the generalization performance of partition-based regression models, specifically addressing limitations in decision trees, clustering algorithms, and density models. A key innovation lies in integrating rich domain knowledge regarding economic and financial wealth dynamics. By exploiting techniques from nonlinear dimensionality reduction, the proposed non-linear feature engineering pipeline mitigates the conflict between model accuracy and generality. Empirical validation utilizing two real-world datasets—World Income and Household Finance—confirms the method's effectiveness.

This paper introduces a straightforward and efficient experimental methodology utilizing a fluence-based closed-loop (FLC) superplonical-mirror system (SLM) for 3D structured light microscopy within biological samples. By iteratively adjusting null-focusing conditions, low-intensity light patterns are projected onto specific volumes, facilitating precise photostimulation and localization of endogenous calcium signals in living zebrafish embryos. Consequently, the light is molded into three predetermined shapes: ellipses, stars, and crosses. Our FLC-SLM architecture allows these figures to be generated concurrently, with individual dimensions and orientations adjustable through real-time feedback. To validate the system's efficacy for patterned photostimulation in tissue, various parameters regarding the fluid dynamics of the ellipses and spatial positioning were tested. The proposed approach offers a cost-effective framework for delivering complex optical patterns into opaque media, a development promising to enhance photostimulation technologies and expand 3D photostimulation methodologies.

Monolithic CMOS sensors utilizing the thinnest achievable active layer technology are a primary objective for high-energy physics experiments aiming to minimize energy loss from particles, thereby maximizing resolution, and suppressing charge dilution to enhance detection accuracy. Nevertheless, this charge dilution effect is affected by factors like hole drift time in the depletion zone. To investigate these influences, a 6-inch diameter 300-$\mu$m thick high-resistivity float-zone silicon-on-insulator (FOZOI) test wafer has been processed into the Monolithic Small Collection Layer technology demonstrator (CLICTD). This demonstration involves etching small circular electrodes (30 $\mu$m in diameter) spaced at 300 $\mu$m intervals across the FOZOI film to study their effects. To better understand charge dilution, a parallel set of 6-inch FOZOI wafers has been thinned to 30, 60, and 150 micrometers, then fabricated into identical Small Collection Layer devices (CLICTD). This work details the fabrication procedures and a detailed characterization of these sensors across the various active layer thicknesses.

We report, for the first time, initial results utilizing the atmospheric self-coherent camera (SCC) technique operating at 80 Hz in a ground-based free-space optical experiment conducted at the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics (SCADAO) laboratory. We also evaluated the relationship between SCC processing rates and observed reductions in SCC-guided laser beam laser-induced wavefront error (ELSE), compared against expected reductions from ideal loop closure theory.

Meta-analyses frequently utilize random-effects models to aggregate independent studies addressing a set of core inquiries. This study introduces a specialized CRRE variant designed to calculate the variance of the fixed-effect coefficients and the predictive interval mean in typical random-effects meta-analyses. We implement this estimator using the bivariate random-effects model for groups of trials influenced by shared design elements. Our approach assumes the summary effect estimates adhere to distinct multivariate normal distributions centered on study-specific parameters, which are then modeled via hierarchical random effects. After deriving the CRRE formulation and its computational algorithm, we evaluate its performance through a simulation study. These experiments demonstrate that the proposed CRRE offers consistently more accurate coverage for 95% predictive intervals compared to standard methods, particularly in scenarios involving small meta-analytic samples and when the data exhibit bivariate skewness. Finally, we apply the methodological framework to a real-world analysis of antipsychotic medications' efficacy and side effects, addressing the previously noted limitations in covering 95% predictive intervals for individual-quality metrics.

Direct penetration impact of a jet of gas within a liquid flowing through a channel triggers disturbances in the jet's surface, which in turn generates turbulence inside both the jet and surrounding flow. This study examines the case where a turbulent jet, characterized by a Reynolds number $Re$ ranging from 100 to 1000, impacts a co-orientated jet (piston flow) also within a confined channel. Measurements acquired via these methods provided velocity profiles, penetration depths, and the characteristics of shear layer instabilities. Ensuring data integrity is crucial for system reliability, a concern that has evolved with the advent of energy-efficient non-volatile main memory. This type of RAM allows data to persist without power, offering significant speed advantages over traditional persistent storage, yet it introduces algorithmic challenges to guaranteeing system consistency. While current solutions depend on expensive slow secondary storage, they are becoming obsolete for High-Performance Computing (HPC) environments due to limited storage throughput and lack of memory capacity to hold persistent layers. Consequently, there is an urgent requirement for consistency algorithms that operate independently of external storage. This work presents the design and implementation of such a solution within HPC databases, tailored to leverage Non-Volatile Main Memory while providing strong consistency guarantees. The proposed algorithm ensures crash consistency according to the practical post-crash consistency model, which mandates that only consistent data snapshots remain accessible after a failure. The system is designed to be efficient, utilizing Non-Volatile Main Memory effectively to absorb write amplification and manage dirty pages during transactions. Benchmark results indicate effective system performance even under heavy loads, with a peak throughput of 10.3 GB/s observed on a system equipped with 256 GB of Non-Volatile Main Memory.

We propose that these diverse outcomes can be unified under a single framework of phase-space density conservation, wherein separations in chaotic encounters and direct predictions regarding bound states arise as complementary facets of this principle.

By employing an energy variational approach, the influence of electron displacement and compression on this state's behavior has been analyzed. Results indicate that electron displacement gives rise to a displacement term within the GHZ Hamiltonian, while compression generates a structure resembling a spin model in the GHZ phase that links to the compass state. It is also noted that this specific phase transition model emerges within the system only when both displacement and compression effects are active simultaneously.

Accurately representing interface geometry is vital for analyzing and simulating multiphase flow phenomena. This study evaluates and contrasts various representation methods, ultimately demonstrating the superior accuracy of using skeleton-based representations over alternatives. To achieve this, we introduce an efficient algorithm capable of generating a skeleton from level set data while maintaining consistent spacing. Furthermore, this representation allows for the concise description of three key geometric attributes—normal direction, curvature, and curvature vector—which are essential for both analysis and computational fluid dynamics modeling.

This paper investigates the fluid mechanical behavior of self-rotating viruses suspended in a fluid. It is well established that certain large, complex biological entities, including some viruses, can drive currents within their surrounding fluid environment. This occurs because their internal motion breaks time-reversal symmetry, allowing them to perform work on the fluid despite translating without a net displacement. By employing flow resistance analysis, this study demonstrates that when the center of mass remains stationary, a biological object of zero net angular momentum will spontaneously rotate in a random orientation if it rotates freely. Furthermore, analyzing the energy dissipation reveals that such self-rotating objects, which maintain their orientation relative to their position, will spontaneously heat up the fluid by converting internal energy into orbital motion. Finally, flow resistance analysis yields an method to detect spontaneous self-rotation of these viruses by observing either their Brownian translation or their Brownian rotation.

*Warped disk* galaxies are defined by a major, non-gravitational interaction that significantly alters their structure. We provide a comparative analysis of two distinct, non-gravitational phenomena affecting disk galaxies: *U-type warps* (where starlight reveals a non-gravitational interaction below the galactic disk's main plane) and the *jellyfish star systems* (where stellar absorption from stars being stripped of the galaxy form the "tear-drop" shape). In this study, we examine the relationship between U-type warps and jellyfish systems within star-forming clusters. We find a high proportion of systems possessing both a U-type warp and a jellyfish system within star-forming clusters (6 out of 8; 75%). This suggests a strong link between the two phenomena, where U-type warps in star-forming clusters are likely the stellar counterpart to the gaseous U-type warps. In this context, the term "gaseous U-type warps" refers to the extended gaseous structures often seen in star-forming clusters.

Applied to the Drude model with finite broadening representing the infinite size of the Fermi sea, the non-adiabatic BEC is found to be half the total electrons present. This constant value remains unchanged regardless of how the metal's density of states evolves.

Results show that minor, incremental adjustments to this coefficient can trigger chaos-induced diffusion, yielding significant shifts in lyapunov exponents. We identify and analyze a specifically "lyapunov singularity point," where infinitesimal alterations in the lag produce drastic outcomes. This study presents a method to derive a stable final conclusion regarding design choices by synthesizing analysis results derived from multiple representation formats (such as diagrams and text) used in engineering discussions. The core issue addressed is the instability of extracted decisions across different analyses, often stemming from discrepancies between diagrammatic and linguistic data. To resolve this variance, we propose diagram-based interpolation of textual insights. By analyzing how diagrams illustrate ideas found in written analyses, we identify diagrammatic features that express these interpretations. The texture analysis is then employed to validate diagrammatic equivalence, ensuring a robust correlation between written descriptions and visual elements. This method stabilizes the extraction process by leveraging diagrammatic analysis to mediate the interpretation of design analyses, resulting in consistent decision-making across mixed modalities.

The broad success of the High-Z cosmological surveys, including DESI, BOSS, and BCC, relies heavily on the spectral cross-correlation (SpCC) technique to infer the statistical properties of astrophysical sources. These techniques depend heavily on template spectra, utilizing a database of spectra from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Survey (APOGEE) to extract geometric correlations among galaxies. However, this approach introduces significant artifacts, primarily the "template bias," which manifests as large oscillations in the one-point correlation function. These artifacts stem from the fundamental mismatch between individual stellar spectra and composite galaxy spectra. To resolve this, the authors propose a new strategy employing a fully probabilistic framework that jointly models the spectrum of a single object with a ensemble of spectral models spanning diverse cosmic parameters. Applied to mock data, the performance of this model is benchmarked against traditional high-Z surveys, revealing a substantial reduction in template bias while preserving critical cosmological information.

Lately, various machine learning models designed to predict how pairs of compounds interact rely heavily on pre-existing knowledge graphs filled with chemical interaction data. These models vary, employing techniques ranging from relational machine learning to deep graph and attention architectures. Despite their differences, a core function common to all is modifying initial drug pair scores by referencing information within these specialized graphs. To understand this shared mechanism, we introduce a unified framework that places these diverse neural architectures on firm theoretical ground. Consequently, this model predicts drug pair properties by fating structural knowledge from chemical knowledge graphs into neural representations, effectively transforming the task into identifying properties of linear combinations of embedded vector pairs. We demonstrate the validity of this approach using public data for the task of identifying potential antibiotics, achieving performance on par with state-of-the-art methods that do not rely on pre-trained graphs but benefit significantly from their usage. Furthermore, our analysis reveals consistent patterns in the learned embeddings and confirms that both training convergence and predictive accuracy are enhanced when knowledge graphs are conditioned to generate high-quality embeddings.

Identifying road damage and implementing repairs are critical municipal responsibilities that enhance public safety, reduce congestion, and lower environmental impacts. Current detection methods primarily depend on visual analysis using on-site vehicles equipped with cameras. Since expert annotators must manually classify damage into specific categories and estimate the distance to each instance to generate accurate labels, collecting training data is often time-consuming and costly. To address these challenges, this study introduces a novel deep learning framework leveraging transfer source models. The proposed system utilizes a source model pre-trained on a large dataset of 10,000 images gathered from 10 different countries to adapt for detecting road defects in a specific target nation. By focusing transfer learning, this approach efficiently trains a compact model with minimal customized labeled data. We compare these results against a model trained using an equivalent amount of damage images uniquely collected from the target country. Furthermore, we evaluate a new preprocessing technique that enhances the visibility of structural elements and amplifies the contrast between lesions and the surrounding pavement. Experiments conducted with a YOLOv4 neural network, employing both pre-training and retraining strategies using a dataset enriched with multiple detection techniques and enhanced with new augmentation strategies, demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms direct training on limited target-specific data.

Mimic learning seeks to transfer expert expertise into learned agent policies. While the standard paradigm relies on an initial batch of mimicked interactions, this paper explores extending an agent's reach across unseen domains by leveraging expert trajectories from various environments. We address cross-domain mimicry—a domain-generalization variant of mimicry—by proposing a new framework that simultaneously refines policy acquisition and world model learning world models. We name this approach "cross-domain imitation from observations" (or CMIFO). The proposed method leverages the implicit knowledge of the expert across multiple domains and utilizes world model predictions to fill in data gaps caused by non-alignment between them. As this is the first system of its kind, we introduce several challenge benchmarks derived from popular gridworlds and a real-world robotics task to test generalization limits. Comprehensive experiments confirm that our approach achieves performance in new domains that rivals or exceeds standard mimicry techniques trained with perfect access to expert data for those specific areas.

A significant challenge in the early universe involves forming the first massive Population III (Pop III) stars, which are generally expected to form in low-metallicity, subatomic mass environments similar to Taurus-class protostars. Specifically, if stars form within circumstellar disks, they may undergo fragmentation, potentially spawning a binary or multiple star system rather than a single star. We applied an exponentially intensified magnetic field model, utilizing the W33 (ω) function, to investigate the impact of magnetic fields on the radial fragmentation of disks surrounding massive Pop III protostars. Our findings indicate that a growing magnetic field can elevate the magnetospheric truncation radius and reduce the magnetospheric radius. Simultaneously, it increases the maximum allowed fragments in a magnetically supported disk, thereby raising the maximum mass of a single star. Notably, a Pop III star formed under a fragmented disk scenario cannot exceed a mass of approximately 30 solar masses ($M_{\odot}$) without external influences, implying that mechanisms like escalating magnetic fields are essential for producing the supermassive Pop III stars observed.

Association rules have become a standard method for extracting insights from association sets [20], [21], [22]. While recent approaches focus on optimizing these extraction methods by identifying redundant rules to prevent duplicate information or by ensuring results remain within an optimal subset of rules, they often overlook the inherent characteristics of redundant rules. This study addresses both the reduction and deduction of redundant rules to achieve superior data compression. First, we examine the specific properties of redundant rules to facilitate more effective redundancy identification. Following this analysis, we introduce a novel algorithm, $S$-based $S$-S, which operates more efficiently than existing solutions. The paper further addresses association rule deduction, enabling the transformation of redundant rules to simplify further processing. Additionally, we present $K$-S, an algorithm capable of identifying the smallest possible set of redundant rules.

Approximately 40% — and potentially as many as 60% — of convicts demonstrate at least one psychological issue, prompting several states to implement therapy mandates within the criminal justice system. Yet, empirical data regarding these interventions remains limited. This research investigates the impact of mandated mental health care on recidivism and public safety among convicted individuals with mental health struggles in California following an in-state legislative requirement introduced in the late 1990s. By comparing outcomes for those with severe versus minor offenses to isolate the treatment effect, the study finds that this policy significantly lowers reincarceration rates for individuals with severe needs while also reducing their presence on the streets within three years of release. Conversely, no statistically significant changes in recidivism or time served were observed for those with minor offenses. Additionally, the implementation resulted in extended prison sentences and increased incarceration rates for offenders with mental health conditions during their peak treatment years. These results suggest that the therapy program effectively mitigates future risk and public danger for those with severe conditions but does not influence recidivism for others; however, the program also appears to function as a nonrecourse option, resulting in additional time lost by recipients with severe needs rather than purely beneficial outcomes.

This paper introduces a parametric variant of the generalized Apostol–Bernoulli polynomials alongside corresponding generating functions of parametric type. We derive various properties and evaluation formulas for these polynomials, with specific focus on establishing types of parametric generalized idempotent polynomials derived from them.

Radio map estimation involves characterizing nonlinear 3-dimensional propagation environments by utilizing collected signal measurements. This challenging task becomes particularly demanding in dynamic settings involving autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), where constraints such as limited onboard energy, memory, and processing capability must be met. To capitalize on real-time data from these flying sensors, we present an online algorithm that jointly optimizes the sensing trajectory and acquisition parameters while ensuring the privacy of the resulting spatial data maps. To support this approach, we first establish a nonlinear analytical model for received signal power that accounts for radio frequency characteristics of specific hardware combinations—including RF transceivers, antenna arrays, and MIMO configurations and their movement through the air. Subsequently, we formulate an optimization problem aimed at maximizing the information gained for channel estimation under strict feasibility bounds for energy, storage, and computational capacity. Ultimately, we demonstrate numerically that our proposed framework outperforms traditional offline methods across all constrained resources.

Recent high-energy physics experiments have detected numerous particle phenomena that challenge the Standard Model's adequacy, signaling the need for new physics beyond its current framework. While much of the community's effort focuses on searching for novel phenomena at large scales, detecting subtle anomalies representing minor deviations from the Standard Model remains a powerful strategy for uncovering traces of emerging physics. This study introduces a novel mathematical framework grounded in hidden Markov models to identify such anomalies, applicable across diverse detector types and readout systems. By leveraging the properties of HMMs, gauge likelihoods are computed for comprehensive experimental datasets. Guides of likelihoods serve as input for various statistical methods to pinpoint regions exhibiting significant deviations, signifying potential anomalies yet to be discovered. The framework's efficacy is validated through simulations of a tracking detector exposed to both uniform background events and mixed backgrounds with distinct astrophysical signals.

This study introduces a novel multimodal biometric dataset, which has been shared for the first time to support the audio-visual-thermal (AVT) modals for person verification. This initiative aims to enhance biometric security by integrating complementary features from AVT sources, effectively mitigating vulnerabilities associated with any single modality. We have conducted comprehensive evaluations of state-of-the-art techniques across all three AVV sources to generate a robust baseline for this new dataset. Furthermore, we perform an in-depth analysis of the results following the combination processes to identify the most effective strategies for person verification systems leveraging AVT data.

Data augmentation is a technique for building larger training sets through artificial generation of samples, thereby enhancing model performance. Although augmentation offers a pathway to improve data-starved NLP applications, it often demands excessive resources, prompting our work to reduce the necessary computational and human investment. We introduce a method that increases available information within audio-translation datasets by injecting pairs of existing sentence translations into neural machine translation models, while simultaneously fine-tuning the resulting aligners using pairs aligned by translation pairs in machine alignment tasks. Crucially, our approach generates new training samples by pairing existing translations within the dataset without introducing synthetic data. We evaluate the neural machine translation system on the CoVid-19 and news translation datasets, and the alignment algorithm on the IterTest dataset. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms baselines that rely solely on synthetic augmentation or that rely solely on the addition of real data to existing corpora.

This study introduces a novel unbiased estimator designed to determine the mean of a distribution parameter from a mixture, based on a limited number of mixed components observed through an imperfect, biased sampling process. The estimator is a generalized maximum likelihood function constructed using self-information derived from the original data and the current hypothesis parameter value because of this dependency on estimation state. A completely recursive algorithm determines this estimator through the sequential incorporation of each new observation, specifically tailored here with a multinomial distribution model to analyze its statistical properties.

This study addresses the challenge of releasing data tables where dependencies exist among columns within the framework of one-sided differential privacy (1-DP). We demonstrate through both the standard inference attack and the maximized inference attack approaches that such dependent structures can substantially amplify attack efficacy. Consequently, depending relations may narrow the protection gap inherent in 1-DP. Under assumptions of binary domain values for table entries, we determine the precise maximum gain achievable through inference attacks targeting any arbitrary dataset structures. For entries restricted to non-negative real values, we establish approximate lower and upper bounds on potential inference improvements across general dependent scenarios; these bounds accurately predict dependent advantages in certain cases. Additionally, recognizing that incriminating specific records offers practical value beyond merely boosting accuracy, we investigate the magnitude by which dependencies accelerate an attacks rate of progression. Surprisingly, for both attack types, certain datasets allow leaks to begin as early as the first element, eliminating any delay in initial data exposure. Finally, we examine how one-sided privacy constraints influence leaks directed exclusively by row headers, providing bound estimates in this context and identifying specific datasets that reveal row values immediately upon observing the first column.

A new disc discovery reveals that the protoplanetary disc surrounding AS 209 contains an inner structure defined by a bright ring located at 70–90 AU, with an outer boundary around 260 AU, separated by a significant gap. To explore the genesis of such features, researchers conducted radiative transfer simulations using the TRAPPIST-1 photometric spectrum under multiple physical models, which successfully reproduce this inner formation. However, the outer formation of such gaps requires more complex models involving dust growth combined with dust entrainment and vertical mixing. Specifically, the dust envelope in AS 209's disc contains only 0.01% by mass within 260 AU, representing a depletion level 100-fold greater than in the inner regions. While dust accumulation at pressure maxima accounts for this deficit in some areas, the inner 70–100 AU zone exhibits 10-fold lower surface brightness, suggesting that volatile processing likely affects this specific gap.

We present an open-source toolbox for analyzing time-tagged data available on request; this software analyzes precisely timed sequences of 'time-tag' events, each assigned to one of multiple channels, to extract the temporal architecture between channels. The utility was developed to evaluate the architecture of time-tagged data available on request; this software analyzes precisely timed sequences of 'time-tag' events, each assigned to one of multiple channels, to extract the temporal arrangements. It was employed to analyze the time-tag tagged signals recorded while applying an electronic stimulation to and accurately acquiring the resulting output when activating an OA with current stimulations. Furthermore, the toolbox evaluates combined measurements of Ca2-tag tagged signals arising from concurrent monitoring of intracellular calcium concentration changes within an OA stimulated with glucose to produce energy.

In previous work titled "A mean field game with control constraints and state restrictions: existence of weak solutions," the lead author established the presence of classical solutions under a set of stringent regularity conditions. Building on this, the current study aims to establish the existence of *mild solutions* by relaxing the regularity requirements. A notable advancement in the present manuscript addresses the absence of a linear control transformation, which was typically employed in prior literature to minimize regularity demands; the author demonstrates that a linear control transformation is unnecessary in the present context.

Stellar filaments are hypothesized to offer insights into the structure of the Galaxy's potential potential well, as well as the pathways through which stars migrate. However, gaps remain regarding how well this hypothesis is supported by data. Using the Gaia DR3 dataset, we analyzed the phase-space arrangements of Gaia-Benchmark 2 stellar filaments. Our findings indicate that these filaments are not confined to narrow, specific features within phase space; rather, they spread extensively, sharing phase-space regions widely with other members of the population under study. Furthermore, we observed that stellar position uncertainties in the spatial domain are sufficiently large to preclude any claims about these filaments forming coherent, planar structures in real physical space. While we acknowledge that the limitations in astrometric precision within current DR3 data restrict the granularity of our analysis, the primary conclusion is that the observed DR3 stellar filaments cannot be interpreted as tangible physical structures.

Selecting items that are stylistically cohesive is crucial for creating appealing outfit proposals, yet it poses significant challenges to automated systems due to the difficulty in establishing stylistic compatibility. Current methods typically rely on on-the-fly learning or domain-specific pre-training. This paper introduces a new approach, VICTOR, designed to rank outfit proposals based by learning from a vast collection of individual garments without requiring pre-labeled groups. VICTOR relies on two core components: a contrastive pre-training strategy tailored to fashion imagery and a novel loss function for handling disjointed bundles of mismatched clothes. Our experimental results demonstrate that VICTOR yields improvements over both prior art relying on disconnected pre-training and systems trained with assembled ready-to-wear sets. Additionally, we evaluate VICTOR using domain transfer tests, DIL, and visual reasoning assessments to DIL demonstrate its potential in enhancing visual reasoning tasks.

Quantum resource theory provides a rigorous framework for evaluating quantum advantages, although its inherent abstract nature can create barriers for newcomers. This review serves as a general introduction, summarizing recent advancements in using rheomatically strict "no-theorems" (such as monotonicity under free operations) to analyze novel phenomena across various physical disciplines. A primary focus lies in distinguishing between classical and nonclassical illumination; while the latter consists solely of classically indexed light modes, it exhibits uniquely quantum behaviors. These include satisfying super-shotnoise intensity correlations, achieving correlations beyond classical limits, and displaying non-Gaussian characteristics, all within a unified resource model. We examine how the absence of classical noise enables these signatures and determines their convertibility into one another within the structured landscape of resource analysis. Drawing specific inspiration from applications in super-sensitive intensity-correlation metrology and machine learning, this perspective aims to demonstrate the broad applicability and elegance of rigorous resource-based approaches.

We introduce a buffer-based asynchronous aggregation approach for distributed training, adapted from a technique originally used in deep reinforcement learning. This method ensures that the final model parameter adheres strictly as an exact linear combination of all client gradients. Unlike previous applications of this technique in Federated Learning (FL), where it was previously believed to require constraints on the number of client updates or gradient norms, we demonstrate that the method functions effectively without any such restrictions on the total number of updates, the order in which they arrive, or their magnitudes. We provide theoretical bounds for communication and computation complexities as well as to estimate communication and storage requirements. Furthermore, we present experimental results showing that this approach is approximately 2.5 times faster than standard synchronous federated learning and operates more than four times quicker than current state-of-the-art federated techniques as optimized in prior research.

This study introduces a new framework called the algebra of polynomial tempered distributions, denoted as $\mathcal{PD}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$, defined as the vector space sum of $m$-th order derivatives where the coefficients belong to the space of polynomials $\mathcal{PD}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. This distribution algebra is constructed by taking the inductive limit of pre-Hilbert spaces equipped with an inner product. Specifically, we define the metric on this space by extending the inner product to an appropriate polynomial basis. Furthermore, we demonstrate that $\mathcal{PD}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ forms a commutative, unital Banach algebra under the convolution operation and provide a functional analysis of this new algebra. Finally, we discuss the multiplicative characters of $\mathcal{PD}(\mathbb{R})$ and derive the corresponding Hausdorff local topology derived from the dual space of $\mathcal{PD}(\mathbb{R})$.

We examine how the mass limit for primordial black holes can be determined using the swampland conjecture, specifically the Refined Distance Conjecture, within an Effective Field Theory (EFT) framework where these holes form immediately after inflation. In the model under study, the inflaton is represented as a light scalar from an extensive tower of tower states (DOS) governed by an exponential potential; this setup also accounts for the cosmological dark energy dominant today. We demonstrate that even at minimal field values, the EFT remains valid up to the present epoch, with the distance scale set by Planckian scales. Consequently, applying the Refined Distance Conjecture reveals an upper bound on the DOS states' mass that decreases exponentially with increasing field values, rather than being limited by the Planckian scales of the Planckian states. We apply this novel approach to investigate the nature of dark matter, specifically calculating the fraction of the total dark matter composed of these DOS states in terms of the model's parameters. We show this proportion can be substantial, potentially accounting for 100% of the dark matter budget. We further discuss the cosmological implications of an abundance of cosmological matter consisting of these primordial black holes.
